package_info.package_versions: Not specified (all versions with vulnerable report_admin.php and host.php code)
package_info.why_malicious: Cacti is vulnerable due to improper handling of user-supplied input in the device name and description fields. The application fails to sanitize or escape these fields before rendering them in the admin reporting interface, enabling attackers to inject persistent JavaScript payloads (stored XSS) that execute in the browser of privileged users. This allows for session hijacking, privilege escalation, and further compromise of the application.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when an admin user views the reports_admin.php page
required_permissions: filesystem (write to DB via web interface)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when an admin views reports_admin.php, the code retrieves the $title and $description fields from the database (populated by user input), concatenates them, and outputs the result directly into the HTML response without escaping, resulting in execution of any embedded JavaScript payloads in the admin's browser.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Directly outputting user-controlled data into HTML without any escaping or sanitization allows attackers to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the victim's session, leading to stored XSS.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal behavior requires all user-supplied data to be escaped or sanitized before rendering in the browser to prevent XSS. Here, the application fails to apply any output encoding or validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Concatenating and displaying database fields is common, but only when proper output encoding (e.g., htmlspecialchars in PHP) is applied to prevent code execution.
key_indicators: Absence of output escaping or sanitization functions (e.g., htmlspecialchars, htmlentities)
Direct concatenation and output of user-controlled variables into HTML
Rendering of device name/description fields in privileged admin interface

execution_context.trigger: User input (device name set via host.php), then at runtime when admin views reports_admin.php
execution_context.file_location: host.php (device name input form, stored in DB)
required_permissions: web application access (authenticated user with Sites/Devices/Data permissions)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At input time, an attacker submits a device name containing a <script> tag via host.php. When an admin later views the reports_admin.php page, the malicious payload is retrieved from the database and rendered unescaped in the HTML, causing the JavaScript to execute in the admin's browser.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Device names should be treated as plain text and never allow embedded HTML or JavaScript. Accepting and rendering such input enables stored XSS attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal device name input should be validated and encoded before storage and output. Here, arbitrary HTML/JS is accepted and rendered, violating input validation and output encoding best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for allowing executable code in device name fields; these should always be plain text.
key_indicators: Presence of <script> or other HTML tags in user-supplied input
Lack of input validation or output encoding on device name field
Execution of user-supplied JavaScript in admin context

attack_chain.action: An attacker with authenticated access submits a device name containing a malicious JavaScript payload via host.php.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious payload is stored in the database.

attack_chain.action: An admin user visits reports_admin.php, which retrieves and renders the device name/description fields from the database without escaping.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious JavaScript executes in the admin's browser (stored XSS).

attack_chain.action: The malicious JavaScript executes in the context of the admin session, enabling account takeover, data theft, or further attacks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: compromise of admin account or further exploitation.

behavioral_signatures: User-supplied input rendered in HTML responses without escaping or sanitization
Presence of <script> or other HTML tags in device name or description fields in the database
Execution of JavaScript in admin interface sourced from database fields
file_indicators: report_admin.php (concatenation and direct output of $title and $description variables)
host.php (device name input form lacking input validation or sanitization)
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to /cacti/host.php with device names containing HTML or JavaScript code
Subsequent GET requests to /cacti/reports_admin.php resulting in script execution in the browser
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for user-supplied input fields (such as device name) that are rendered in HTML responses without proper escaping or sanitization. Scan database fields for suspicious patterns such as <script> tags or other HTML/JS content. Use web application firewalls (WAF) to detect and block requests containing potential XSS payloads. Review source code for direct output of user-controlled variables into HTML without encoding. Monitor browser console logs and security events for unexpected script execution in admin interfaces.
